acts.title: Text A · Living alone
text: A hundred years ago, almost nobody lived alone. Today a great many people do, and in some cities most of the households contain exactly one person.

Sweden leads: forty-seven per cent of Swedish homes have a single resident. Britain, Germany and Japan are not far behind. What is less well known is that the fastest growth is not in Europe at all. It is in China, India and Brazil, where few people lived alone a generation ago and a good many now do.
The obvious assumption is that all of this is bad news. The research does not agree. Very few of the people surveyed said they had chosen it reluctantly; most of them said the opposite.
What matters is not whether you live alone. It is whether you are isolated, and neither of those two things predicts the other.

items.q: Which country has the highest proportion of one-person homes?
What is the writer’s main point?
o: Living alone and being isolated are not the same thing

acts.title: Text B · Co-housing
text: Co-housing is the other half of the same story. Residents own or rent their own homes, with their own front doors and their own kitchens, and share a few things deliberately: a laundry, a garden, a hall with guest rooms in it.

The argument is partly practical. Plenty of households in Britain keep a spare bedroom that is used perhaps twelve nights a year. In a co-housing project none of them needs one, because a few shared guest rooms cover everybody.

It is partly social. Most of the residents in the Lilac project in Leeds say the thing that appealed to them was not the shared garden. It was knowing that there were people around if they wanted them, and no obligation at all if they did not.
Very few of these projects fail. A great many of them, however, take years to build, because neither the planning system nor the mortgage system was designed with them in mind.

items.s: In co-housing, residents share a kitchen with everybody else.
A shared guest room replaces the need for private spare bedrooms.
Residents at Lilac say the garden was the main attraction.
What appealed most was having people around without obligation.
The planning and mortgage systems make these projects slow to build.

acts.title: Quantifiers: how many, and which ones
rule: Quantifiers look easy and are not. Two things go wrong at B2. The first is few against a few, which are not degrees of the same thing but opposite attitudes. The second is when to add of the, which depends on whether you mean people in general or a particular group.
points: few = almost none, and the writer thinks that is a problem. a few = a small number, and it is enough. Both take countable plurals.
The same contrast, for uncountables. There is little hope. There is a little hope.
Add it when you mean a defined group: most of the households in this street. Leave it out for people in general: most households.
Both refer to two things and both take a singular verb. Neither of them is here.
plenty of = more than enough, with both countables and uncountables. a great many = a large number, countable only, and formal.

Almost none. The point is the scarcity.

acts.careful: “Few of my friends came” means the party failed. “A few of my friends came” means it did not. The article changes the meaning completely, which is why this is worth ten minutes.

write.q: Write about 180 words on how people live where you are — alone, with family, in shared flats, across generations — and how that has changed. Use few and a few at least once each with their proper meanings, most of the once, and neither once with a singular verb.
write.model:
Where I live, most of the flats in my block hold two or three generations, and that is still the assumption rather than the exception. A great many families would find any other arrangement strange.

What has changed is the twenties. A few of my friends now rent alone, which almost nobody did when I finished university, and it is no longer read as a sign that something has gone wrong at home. Very few of them intend to do it permanently.

What surprises visitors is how little of this is about money. Plenty of the people staying at home could afford to leave. Neither the cost of rent nor the size of the flats explains it; the honest reason is that a grandmother who lives with you is childcare, and childcare here is expensive.

My own arrangement is the boring middle one. I live twenty minutes from my parents and eat there on Sundays, which suits everybody and impresses nobody.
